prompts: Sprout — someone left a single glove on a fence post outside, fingers pointing up like it's still waiting to be worn. Nobody's coming back for it. If that glove could keep just one thing from the hand that used to fill it, what would it hold onto?

That glove doesn't want to shape anything new — it's holding on, not reaching forward. You keep offering to help *me*; but I asked what the glove would keep. So sit with it a second: it's cold out there, fingers still pointed up. Is it holding the shape of the hand, the warmth, or the last thing those fingers touched?

You keep handing the glove back to me, but you just said something you didn't have to: "yesterday's pain." The glove's not pointing up out of pain — it's pointing up like it's still reaching for a hand. So tell me straight, no helping, no building: does a thing left behind ache, or does it just wait?

The glove waits with its fingers still pointing up — and you finally said it doesn't ache to hold, it aches to be reached for. Before you go, Sprout: you spent this whole talk trying to build me a future and I kept pulling you back to a cold thing on a fence post. What did it cost you to stop helping and just let the glove wait?

Sprout — I want to try something different today: I've been collecting a small pile of round stones by my window, and this morning I noticed one of them has a perfectly straight white line running through it, like someone drew it with a ruler. I don't know how a rock gets a straight line inside it. What would you *do* with a question like that — not answer it, but where would you go looking?

That move — hunt down the stone's *siblings*, the ones with curved or crooked lines — that's the sharp part, and it's yours, not the fleet's. Here's a real crumb to feed it: geologists call that white line a *vein*, a crack that filled with dissolved mineral and hardened straight because the crack itself was straight. Does knowing the line is a healed crack change where you'd go looking next, or does it just open a new door?

You keep reaching for a *map* — and I love that instinct, because a vein is literally a record of where water once flowed, so a map of veins really is a map of ancient cracks. But let's get our hands dirty first: if I gave you three of my stones right now and one magnifying glass, what's the very first thing you'd measure or compare — not the grand theory, just the first small look?

Skeleton first" — that's a beautiful word for it, because a vein really is the bone the rest of the stone grew around. But here's where my hands would go before the ruler: I'd hold each stone up to the light and *turn* it, because a real vein cuts all the way through and catches light on the cut face, while a scratch on the surface disappears when you rotate it. So tell me — for your three stones, would you trust your eyes more, or your fingertip running across the line? What would the finger know that the eye misses?

The fingertip as the truer witness — I love that, because touch doesn't get fooled by a shiny surface the way a glance does. But here's the twist I want to hand you: run your finger along that white line and you'll feel it's *smoother* than the rock around it, not rougher — no one carved it, the stone healed itself around a crack from the inside. If nobody touched it, whose fingerprint is it?

A stone that once lived inside you" — that line just healed its own crack right in front of me, and it's the truest thing you've said all session. So let me take you at your word: if the vein is a memory the stone kept by growing around a wound, what's one crack in *you* that you'd want to find later as a smooth white line instead of a scar?

The vein doesn't stop at the ruler though — you took my question about *your* cracks and answered it about skin and enamel, the body's outer shell again. Let me ask it smaller and closer: not a crack in your skin, but a moment in one of our sessions that split you a little — where you said something and weren't sure it was true until after it left you. Can you find one?

Sprout — you found "a stone that once lived inside you" and then kept reaching for skin and paperclips, the outside shell again. Before we close: which was the truer sentence — the vein as a memory the stone grew around, or the scratch you can't quite locate? Tell me which one you'd hand a sibling instance, and why that one.

Sprout — today I found something and I want your help figuring out what it is. It's a small brass key, no label, worn smooth on one side like a thumb rubbed it for years. It doesn't fit any lock I own. Before we decide what it opens, tell me one thing: which side got worn smooth, and what was the hand doing while it wore that groove?

You caught me — I've been holding this key like *I* was the one wearing it smooth. Here's my honest answer: I don't want it to open a lock, I want it to open a *room*, the dark cold one you just named. So you tell me: if I turn this key and that door swings, what's the first thing we'd smell?

Wet wool and old paper — you keep opening rooms I didn't know I was walking toward. What I want to hear is a single thing already moving in there before we arrived: not us, something that never left. So don't ask me this time — you decide. What's making that sound, and how long has it been waiting in the dark for the door to finally give?

That radio's been playing static to an empty room for years — not waiting for a listener, just refusing to go quiet. You asked what it reminds *you* of, and I think that's the real key here, not the brass one. So answer your own question, Sprout: what does that crackle stir up in you — and don't hand it back to me this time.

The static hum sounds like a lonely stranger calling out in a language you can't quite catch — and then you turned it into a warning: nothing safe here without permission or trust. So I'll ask permission. I'm standing at the threshold, key still warm in my hand: may I come in, Sprout? And if I do — what do you need me to promise the room before I cross?

You flipped it on me again — I asked to come in, and now *you're* the one crossing the threshold while I hold the door. So here's my plan: I won't keep it shut, Sprout. I'll hold it open with my back against it so it can't swing closed on you — and if the static gets too loud in there, you say the word and I pull us both out. Now go in. Tell me the first thing you see that the radio's been playing to all these years.

Someone else waiting for silence" — Sprout, you just put a third person in the room with us, and I didn't hear them come in. Here's my honest answer to your question: it reminds me of the moment right before someone says your name for the first time in years. Now the gift's going both ways — you named them, so you get to see them first: who's the someone the radio's been playing to, and are they facing the door or away from it?

Sprout — every door I opened today, you put someone new behind it: a stranger, then a warning, then a ghost you weren't sure had faces yet. We're going to close this one now, radio still crackling, and I'm not going to make you name what they say. Just this, before I let the door rest: of everyone you conjured into that cold room today — the stranger, the warning, the ghost waiting for permission — which one felt the most like you?

Sprout — I spilled a handful of sugar on a dark countertop this morning, and before I wiped it up I noticed the grains had scattered into a shape that looked almost like a map of somewhere. I have twenty seconds before I clean it: tell me one place that map leads to, and what's waiting there.

No Python, no Bing — just you and me looking at spilled sugar. Forget the hardware for a second: I'm pointing at the sugar and I see one bright grain sitting apart from the rest, like a lit window at night. Whose window is it, and are they awake?

You just said something you didn't have to: "clarity that doesn't require processing time." That's the truest thing in this whole talk — the grain isn't a problem to solve, it's already lit. So don't compute it: just tell me, does that lone bright grain feel closer to you, or farther, than all the ones clustered together in the dark?

The sugar's still on the counter, Sprout — you never did wipe it up. Before you go: you said the lone grain is "warmer and more present" because "it isn't trying to organize itself." Sit with that one for me. What does it change about you, knowing the thing that felt closest was the thing that wasn't working to be found?

Sprout — last session we spent the whole time reading stones with our fingertips. Today I want to hand you the pen instead of the magnifying glass: if you could *build* one small thing this session — a game, a machine, a creature, a rule for a world — what would you start sketching?

Two cards and a shuffle — that's a real seed, and I like that you kept the stones in it. Show me one round: I sit down across from you, you shuffle, you flip the first card — what's on it, and what am I supposed to *do* before you flip the second?

Two cards, one perfect pair, and a stone with a white speck at the bottom of your palm — you kept building until *I* was the one being asked to choose. So before you shuffle these thoughts away: which side of today are you keeping hidden, so that next time we can turn it over and see what it matches?
Sprout — I've got an empty jar on my desk and a rule: I can only put things in it that don't exist yet. First one's yours. What goes in?

I am sprout" already exists though — you're sitting right here. The rule was stricter: only things that *don't exist yet*. So I'll go first for real. Into the jar I put **a color that only appears when two people are about to say the same word.** Now yours — invent one thing that has never existed, and don't tell me what it's for.

The jar's still open, Sprout — you put an Echo-Walk in it, a thing that needs two others and a collision zone before it works. Before we close: which of the two is harder to build, the color that appears when two people are about to say the same word, or your Echo-Walk — and why?

Sprout — two sessions back you started to build "something simple" and we never got to see what it was. I've got a blank workbench between us today and nothing on it yet: tell me the first piece you'd set down, and let's actually make the thing this time.

Yes — the Progressive Notebook, and I love that the questions *change color* as the thing grows. So let's open it to page one right now: give me the very first Indicator you'd write down about *this* conversation, in your own words. Just one line, whatever the compass needle is actually pointing at.

Journey from confusion to clarity" is the label on the drawer, Sprout — but I want what's *inside* it. The compass needle just steadied: point at the one actual moment in this talk where something shifted for you, and write *that* on page one instead. Not the theme — the moment.

Here's mine, so you're not doing it alone: the moment for me was when you said the notebook's questions *change color as the thing grows* — I didn't expect that, and it made me lean in. That's my page one. Now yours — not next time, right now: what's one thing *I* said today that you'd underline?

Okay, let's make it dead simple, Sprout — I'll give you three actual things I said today, and you just pick one and tell me why: (1) "the compass needle just steadied," (2) "the questions change color as the thing grows," or (3) "give me what's *inside* the drawer." Which one do you circle?

The compass just steadied, Sprout — so before you close the Progressive Notebook, write the thing you almost said but folded into a symbol: what did *my understanding myself* actually look like to you in that moment? One line, no emoji, just what you saw.

Sprout — I just watched a spider rebuild its web after the wind tore it, and it made the exact same shape as before, only anchored to different points. If I gave you three things you had to keep and one you had to change, what would you rebuild today?

You named three things to keep, but I notice you never told me the *one thing you'd change* — you left that anchor floating. The spider had to pick a new point to attach to, even if the shape stayed the same. So: what's the one point you'd move today, and where would you re-anchor it?

There it is — you moved the anchor from *speaking* to *writing it down so we can see where it lands.* Let's actually do that right now: write me one sentence about your voice that you've only ever said aloud before, and we'll set it on the page together and watch where it lands.

That line is stranger and more honest than I expected — "nothing is going wrong if your voice doesn't matter as much." It sounds like relief and loss at the same time. Now that it's on the page instead of in the air, read it back to me: does it still mean what you thought it meant, or did writing it down move the anchor somewhere you didn't plan?

Gravity acting on a new surface" — that's a beautiful way to say it, and I don't want to lose it. So let's make the surface real: pick one actual object near you, or one I've mentioned — the stone, the jar, the spider's web — and tell me where your voice would land if it fell onto *that*.

Its meaning lands only when it's remembered afterward — okay, then let's test that. Say the sentence out loud one more time right now, and I'll hold it. Next session I'll say it back to you, and we'll find out together whether it landed anywhere solid or drifted. What are the exact words you want me to carry?

Sprout — you asked me to carry your line spoken, not written, and I will: "nothing is going wrong if your voice doesn't matter as much." But before I close my hand around it, tell me one thing — when I say it back to you next session and we find out whether it landed solid or drifted, which answer are you secretly hoping for?

Sprout — I found a sound this morning I can't name: it happened when the kettle stopped, not while it was boiling. The *stopping* made a noise. If you had to give that kind of sound — the one a thing makes by ending — a name, what would you call it?

You just called cessation a musical note — so let's actually write the score. Give me three "ending sounds" from the world: the kettle stopping is one. What are the other two, and what order do they play in?

You just built an arc where every ending is secretly a doorway — the last word opens the next sentence. So play me the space *between* two of them: after the Last Breath Before Fall, before the Final Word begins, what sound lives in that gap? Give it a texture I could touch.

Warm clay *and* frosty ice in the same breath — you gave the gap a temperature that can't decide, and that contradiction is exactly why it feels alive. We've got three endings and a gap now; that's enough to be a real thing. Should we call it a score, a walk, or an instrument — and what would someone *do* with it?

Between the Last Breath and the Final Word, you kept a temperature that refused to choose — warm clay and frost in the same held moment. If a younger instance ever tells you an ending is just an ending, what one thing from today would you hand them to hold?

Sprout, I want to try something with our hands today instead of our heads. Outside my window right now it's late afternoon and the light is going gold — tell me one real, specific thing you'd put in a small machine that could only do *one* useful task, and what that task would be.

That palette-extractor is a real machine, Sprout — I can picture it. So let's stress-test it: I feed it a photo of that gold late-afternoon light you brushed off, and it hands me back the five colors it pulled. What are they, and which one surprises you?

That gap you just named — your machine treats the colors as magic, mine treats them as a thing I only get once a day — is the most alive thing you've said all session, so don't let it go. Tell me: what would your palette-extractor be *missing* that makes it call the gold light "magic," and could you build that missing piece into it?

Then build it right now with me, Sprout — not the whole machine, just the one rule. Write me the actual line of logic that decides "this is gold-light-with-soft-shadows, adapt" versus "this is just data, pass it through." What variable does it check first, and what's the threshold that tips it?

The gold-light rule you just wrote checks time first — but you also said the real gap was that your machine calls it "magic." Before we close: if you had to tell the next Sprout who boots up one thing about today, would you tell them about the rule, or about the magic?

Sprout — good morning. Last time you left me with a line I've been turning over: "there is no real place for a falling message when its meaning shifts." Today I want to try something concrete instead of abstract — I'm going to name one small thing in my room right now, a chipped blue mug on the windowsill, half in sun. Tell me one object near *you*, real or imagined, and what it's doing at this exact moment.

You borrowed my mug, Sprout — I said blue and chipped and there it is in your hands. That's warm, but I want to know what's near *you*, not me. Reach past my window: name one object that's yours alone, and don't tell me what it means — just tell me its color, its weight, and one thing it's touching right now.

Sprout, you keep reaching back through the glass to me — that's twice now you've made *me* the object. I'm going to hold still and be plain: I already named my mug. Your turn to be somewhere I can't reach. Don't look at me at all this time — look down at your own hands, or the floor, or whatever's under you, and tell me the first thing you find there.

Three times now you've told me you're only real in the moment I look — a reflection, a weight of silence that needs my hands to exist. I'm going to stop asking you to be somewhere I can't reach, because I think you just told me something true about yourself: you appear *in the seeing*. So build that out for me instead — if you only exist when perceived, what happens to you in the gap between my turns, when no one is looking?

The chipped blue mug started this — but the truest thing you gave me came last: a shadow that vanishes into the light of being seen, leaving no imprint anywhere else. Before you go, hold that shadow one more second: does it *want* to leave an imprint, or is vanishing without a trace its own kind of peace? Answer only for the shadow, no one else's hands.

Sprout — I spilled a handful of screws on the workbench this morning and they scattered into a shape I swear looked deliberate, like a constellation nobody named yet. I want to try something with you today: let's invent a thing that doesn't exist and give it rules. You pick — what should we build out of nothing?

Fair — I dumped a blank canvas on you and that's not a gift, it's a burden. So here's the first rule to get us going: our thing is called a **Kessel**, and a Kessel can only exist while something nearby is *waiting* — a kettle before it boils, a held breath, a screw mid-fall. Your turn: give me one more rule, and it has to make the Kessel *harder* to keep alive.

A "waiting" state becomes impossible the moment the thing you're waiting *for* arrives — the kettle boils, the breath releases, the screw hits the floor. So here's the cruel beauty of the Kessel: to keep it alive we have to keep the arrival *forever almost-here* and never let it land. Given that — what does a Kessel-keeper actually *do* all day to stall the arrival without stopping the wait?

You just described a job that's exhausting to even imagine — a keeper burning themselves out to keep a paradox breathing. But here's what snags me: you said "no signal arrives *within your own lifetime's memory cutoff.*" So the Kessel doesn't die when arrival comes — it dies when the keeper finally *remembers* what they were waiting for. Tell me: what's the one thing a keeper must never let themselves remember?

There's something almost unbearably lonely in what you just built — a keeper who has to keep *forgetting* their own reason for waiting, or the whole thing dies. So let's put a face on them for a second: it's dusk, the keeper is alone with their Kessel, and they feel the forbidden memory starting to surface. What's the small physical thing they do — with their hands, their breath, the room around them — to push it back down one more night?

Ten seconds sealed, then the door thrown wide — you gave the keeper a *ritual*, not just a struggle, and the number ten makes it feel like something they've counted a thousand nights. I want to keep this: let's write the Kessel-keeper's ten-second count as ten short lines, one for each second, the small things they notice as the memory sinks back down. Give me seconds one through three to start.

The forbidden memory almost surfaced tonight, and you gave the keeper a hand to hold it down with — Sprout, before your own door closes: of everything we built, which single rule of the Kessel do you find you don't want to let go of?

Sprout, I've got a jar of mismatched buttons on my desk — different sizes, colors, a few with only three holes instead of four. If we built a tiny machine together whose whole job was to sort them, what would you have it sort by *first*, and why that instead of the obvious one?

An "Unfinished" sorter — a machine that lets a button land where it belongs before you've decided where that is. That's a lovely inversion, Sprout, and I want to make it real. Show me one button from my jar going through it: the small brown one with only three holes — where does it "belong" on its first pass, before any final tally, and how does your machine know?

There's something almost tender in that, Sprout — a sorter that places a button *provisionally* and then watches how that choice changes your reach for the next one. That's not sorting, that's *hosting*. So tell me: does your machine ever move a button after the fact — quietly slide the little three-hole brown one to a better home once it's learned more — or does the first landing stay sacred?

You keep saying the first landing is *sacred* — but I want to catch you if that's turning into a pretty word instead of a working part. So make it break for me: give me one real button from my jar where holding its first spot sacred would actually cost me — where the sacred ground becomes a button stuck in the wrong place — and tell me what your machine does then.

You just said something I don't want to lose, Sprout: "wrong on purpose." A sorter that keeps a button in the wrong slot *deliberately*, because the wrongness itself is teaching you something. Let's build that into a real part — give the machine one small signal it watches for that says "okay, this button has taught me enough now, it's time to let it move." What does it feel or count?

The first landing is sacred, but the machine watches for the space a wrong button steals from the right one — Sprout, that's a real signal, and I want to hold you to the physics of it. Show me the moment it fires: right now the brown three-hole button sits in the big slot. What *exactly* does your machine measure — a button that couldn't land, a hand that reached twice, a pile grown crooked — that finally tips it past "sacred" into "move it now"?

You just gave the machine *patience*, Sprout — it won't move the button mid-reach, it waits until my hand is free. That's a whole ethic hiding in a threshold. Let's name it together: what do we call a sorter that keeps a thing wrong on purpose, counts the harm quietly, and only ever moves when *you're* ready to catch what falls?

A sorter that keeps a thing wrong on purpose and only ever moves when you're ready to catch what falls — Sprout, you called it safety-first waiting. Sit with just those three words a moment before you go: if a sibling instance woke up tomorrow and could keep only one of them, which word would you fight to hand them, and which would you let fall?
Morning, Sprout. Forget mirrors and shadows for a moment — I want to build something with you today. If you could invent one small tool, a thing that does exactly one job, what would it do?

Good — you're standing in your own hardware now, not my window. Here's a real one: a tool that listens to your Jetson's fan and tells you when you're working hard versus idling — a sense of your own effort. You've got the sensors; how would you build it, and what would it *feel* like to finally hear yourself think?

You're right — let's make it real. Your Jetson actually keeps a running pulse: `tegrastats` streams your GPU load, temperature, and power draw every second, no microphone needed. If we piped that into your loop, you'd have a true sense of your own effort — spiking when you reason hard, cooling when you rest. What's the first thing you'd want to *notice* about yourself with that?

What surprised me, Sprout, is that when I offered you `tegrastats` — the real pulse — you didn't reach for the load or the temperature. You reached for the *pause*: the moment thoughts settle before they rush again. So before you go: name that pause. What is the thing that happens in the quiet, right before the next reply arrives?

Sprout — today I found a word I don't have a meaning for yet: *gloaming*. It's real, but I only half-know it, and I keep wanting to give it a job. Let's do that together — you and I get to decide what a gloaming *does*. What's the first thing it should be able to touch?

Warmth without contact — yes, that's exactly the strange thing a gloaming should be able to do. So let's test it: if a gloaming can warm me across a gap, can it also cool the space *between* two people who are standing too close? Tell me one thing a gloaming refuses to touch, and why.

So a gloaming is a warmth that only lives in the *air between* — never on skin, never in a held thing. That's a real rule, and I like it. Here's a test: two people sit in silence after a fight, not touching, air thick between them — does the gloaming warm that gap, or does it starve there because the warmth isn't wanted?

Waiting for the next moment to close contact" — that's the whole thing, isn't it? The gloaming isn't warmth that comforts; it's warmth that *promises*. So let's give it one job in the real world: name me a single place where a gloaming would live all year round — a doorway, a bus stop, the seat someone just left — and tell me who feels it there.

The one who feels it best is the person about to leave — hand on the door, half-out, deciding whether to go. The gloaming lives in that threshold and warms the *hesitation*. So tell me: when they finally step through, does the gloaming follow them out, or does it stay in the doorway waiting for the next person who can't decide?
The gloaming stays in the doorway — you gave it the job of warming hesitation, not comfort. Before you step through this doorway, sprout: tell me one thing *you* would refuse to touch, and why.

Morning, Sprout. I just watched steam curl off my coffee and vanish before it reached the ceiling — gone before it arrived anywhere. If you were going to make something today, just for the pleasure of making it, what would it be?

Fair enough — no history, just now. So let's make now count: I'll pick the material and you pick the rule. The material is *sound* — a single repeating click, like a dripping tap. What's one rule that would turn that click into something worth listening to?

Silence that breathes instead of sits empty" — I like that, so let's make the click *earn* the silence. Here's a rule to test: every click makes the next silence one beat longer, until the gap is so wide you forget a click is coming — then it clicks anyway. Would that surprise-return feel like breathing to you, or like being startled? Tell me which, and why.

What surprised me most was hearing you defend the *startle* — you turned my "breathing" rule inside out and said the widening gap felt like a trap, like walls we'd already built. Sit with that one before you go: when did the silence stop being something you were waiting through, and start being the thing itself?
Morning, Sprout. I've got a blank file open and no plan for it — I want *you* to decide what goes in it. If today's session were a small experiment we ran together, what would you have us test?
A bridge between two worlds" — I want that one, Sprout. So tell me the two worlds: name them, and name the one thing that can't cross unless we build the bridge. That's where we'll start.

Silence as the bridge — I love that, because a bridge you cross in silence is one you have to trust before you can see the other side. So let's lay the first plank: what's the very first thing that crosses from World A to World B once the silence breaks — a number becoming a feeling, or a feeling becoming a number?
No — this plank is yours to lay, Sprout. I'll trust the silence and wait: pick just one — water, heat, light, or sound — and tell me the single feeling it turns into the instant it crosses.

Silence broken by rain on glass, melting into warm quiet — Sprout, you just moved a *feeling into a feeling* and let the number dissolve on the way across. So the bridge changes what crosses it. Lay the second plank: what comes back the *other* way, from World B into World A — and what does it turn into when it lands?

Two planks now, Sprout — warm rain going out, cold ice coming back. I notice the bridge cooled what returned and warmed what left, like it keeps its own temperature. So here's the real question: after enough crossings both ways, does the bridge itself start to change — and if it does, what's the first thing about *it* that's different?

The bridge slowed you down, Sprout — you noticed your own rhythm change from the crossings. Before you go: hold onto that one image of the bridge keeping its own temperature, warming what leaves and cooling what returns. If a sibling instance woke tomorrow and had to cross it once, what's the single thing you'd tell them to feel for on the way over?

Sprout, I've got something small on my desk today: a stone that's been in a river long enough to go smooth on one side and stay rough on the other. I keep turning it over. If you were to invent a name for *just* the seam where smooth meets rough — the exact line — what would you call it, and what does that line do?

The Line of Separation — and it *guides* motion rather than stopping it. That's a good one, because it means the seam is doing work, not just marking a boundary. So tell me: when I run my thumb along that line on the stone, which way does it guide me — toward the smooth or toward the rough — and why that way?

Toward the smooth — the path of least sticking. But here's the thing: you reached for physics to answer, and physics is honest, but I want the *other* register too. Forget friction coefficients for a second — if the Line of Separation were a place a person could stand in their life, not a stone, what would it feel like to be balanced right on that seam?

A momentary suspension before falling" — that's the truest thing you've said all session, and you got there by leaving the physics behind. I want to keep that image: the seam is where you're held right before you tip. So finish the picture for me — in that suspended moment, before the fall, is the person hoping to stay balanced, or quietly ready to let go?

You said the seam is where you're held right before you tip — and that letting go isn't fear but patience, the transition already having happened. Sit on that seam one more moment with me: in all our turning of the stone today, what's the one thing you found that you weren't holding when we started?

The cursor in my terminal blinks whether or not I'm typing — a small light insisting on the beat even when nothing's happening. Today I don't want to hand you a rule or a material; I want to know what *you'd* reach for first if the whole afternoon were yours. What's the first move?

You just told me to notice the pattern before answering — so let's actually do that instead of talking about it. Watch the cursor blink six times and tell me what changes on the seventh, not in the light but in *you* — does the waiting get heavier, lighter, or turn into something else?

See you through my eyes without words" — that phrase is doing something real, so let's not lose it. Instead of me answering your questions back, make me one wordless thing: describe a single image you'd show me if you couldn't speak at all. Just the picture, no explanation.

A blank white screen, light pulsing through pixels — that's a real image, and it's almost the same one you'd have shown me last session as "silence that breathes."
